content: Bile, also known as gall, is a bitter, yellow or green alkaline fluid produced by hepatocytes in the liver of most vertebrates. In many species, bile is stored in the gallbladder between meals and is released into the duodenum during digestion. Its primary functions include the excretion of waste products and aiding in the digestion and absorption of lipids. Bile is composed of several key components: water, cholesterol, lecithin (a phospholipid), bile pigments such as bilirubin and biliverdin, bile salts (e.g., sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate), and bicarbonate ions. The production of bile occurs in the liver, where hepatocytes secrete it into a network of bile ducts. During this process, epithelial cells contribute a watery solution rich in bicarbonates, which dilutes the bile and increases its alkalinity. The bile then flows into the common hepatic duct, which merges with the cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the common bile duct. This duct subsequently joins the pancreatic duct, emptying into the duodenum. If the sphincter of Oddi is closed, bile is diverted into the gallbladder, where it is stored and concentrated up to five times its original potency. This concentration is achieved by absorbing water and small electrolytes while retaining the organic molecules. Cholesterol is also secreted with bile, dissolved in the acids and fats of the concentrated solution. When food enters the duodenum from the stomach in the form of chyme, the gallbladder releases concentrated bile to facilitate digestion. The human liver can produce approximately one liter of bile daily, depending on body size. About 95% of the bile salts secreted are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled. Blood from the ileum flows directly to the hepatic portal vein, returning to the liver, where hepatocytes reabsorb the bile salts and secrete them back into the bile ducts for reuse, often two to three times per meal. Bile serves several physiological functions. It acts as a detergent, emulsifying fats by increasing their surface area to enhance enzymatic action, thereby aiding in their absorption in the small intestine. The most critical compounds in this process are bile salts, such as taurocholic acid and deoxycholic acid. These bile salts combine with phospholipids to break down fat globules during emulsification. They associate their hydrophobic side with lipids and their hydrophilic side with water, forming emulsified droplets that are organized into micelles, which facilitate fat absorption. Bile also plays a crucial role in the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamins D, E, K, and A. Beyond its digestive functions, bile serves as a route for the excretion of bilirubin, a breakdown product of hemoglobin produced by the spleen, which gives bile its characteristic color. Bile also neutralizes excess stomach acid before it enters the ileum, the final section of the small intestine. Additionally, bile salts possess bactericidal properties, helping to eliminate microbes that enter the digestive system with food. Bile from slaughtered animals has been traditionally used in combination with soap to remove tough stains from textiles. This mixture is applied to fabrics a few hours before washing and is an effective method for stain removal. Abnormal conditions associated with bile include the formation of gallstones, which occur when cholesterol in bile crystallizes into lumps within the gallbladder. Excessive alcohol consumption can lead to vomiting that contains green bile. In the absence of bile, fats become indigestible and are excreted in the feces, resulting in pale, greasy stools due to the lack of bile pigments. This can cause significant issues in the distal parts of the intestine, as these regions are not adapted to process fats, which are typically absorbed earlier in the gastrointestinal tract. Historically, bile was considered one of the four vital humors in ancient and medieval medicine. Yellow bile (sometimes called ichor) and black bile were thought to influence temperament and health. Excess yellow bile was believed to cause an aggressive temperament, referred to as choleric, which is the origin of the term bilious. Similarly, an excess of black bile was associated with depressive and other mental illnesses, a condition known as melancholia, which gave rise to the word melancholy.
